Screenshot the scoreboard at phase open, mid-phase and close. Build a real performance record. Rotate front-line rally leads. The reserve-first rule Resource events are the easiest place to damage your alliance's AvA performance. The fix is a written reserve floor: Event budget = current stockpile − AvA reserve floor If the event budget is small, score small. A tier-2 reward is not worth entering the next duel with an empty bank. Alliances only win with a plan. docs.content: Six four-hour rounds, rotating themes and a daily milestone ladder. Turn the round clock into a personal action queue and stop wasting scored actions outside their window. docs.title: Advanced Player Progression
docs.description: For accounts past the basics: measure points per resource, build depth instead of power, and design a week that scores in three systems at once.
docs.content: For accounts past the basics: measure points per resource, build depth instead of power, and design a week that scores in three systems at once. Advanced accounts stall for different reasons: not lack of resources, but lack of conversion efficiency and event stacking. The next gains come from measurement, roster depth and deliberate overlap. advanced efficiency event overlap roster depth planning Measure points and value per resource, not raw totals. Build a second and third squad for multi-front events. Pre-plan overlap windows across Survival Battle, AvA and state events. Protect a closer reserve for coordinated finishes. Remove low-value habits, not just add high-value ones. Build a simple spend ledger: date, event, action, resource cost, points. Rank your top five resource conversion paths by points per unit. Identify one alliance role beyond damage dealing: caller, scout, analyst. Plan a weekly overlap map before the reset. Test one new composition per week with a controlled battle report. Run a monthly after-action review and delete one bad habit. The best players are not the biggest spenders; they are the most efficient converters. Depth lets an alliance contest two objectives without collapsing one. A measured small improvement each week compounds faster than a rebuild every month. Record the version and date next to every conclusion. Delegate documentation. An alliance's memory should not live in one person's head. Optimising for power score instead of battle outcomes and event points. Building a second squad without the resources to sustain it. Spending the closer reserve at midday. Treating a single battle report as proof. Ignoring lower-power members who provide coverage and coordination. Planning events from memory instead of a written overlap map. Build the ledger Record every significant spend with points and resource cost. After two weeks you will know your true conversion rates. Design the overlap week Map Survival Battle themes, AvA phases and state events on one board. Mark every action that scores twice. Build depth, not width Improve the second squad only where it unlocks a second front. Depth without sustain is just more losses. Phase-specific stockpiles Six-day coverage Core Closer reserve 10–20% of budget Core Second squad Functional High Battle reports 10+ dated samples High Alliance ledger Updated weekly High Once your account can produce resources reliably, the limiting factor becomes conversion . Points per speed-up, damage per resource, reward per event hour. Measure those, and you will outperform bigger accounts. From power to conversion Track these five metrics: 1. Points per speed-up by event phase. 2. Battle delta per resource for your main composition. 3. Production efficiency (actual vs. potential output). 4. Event reward value in speed-up equivalents. 5. Closer reserve utilisation (spent / held). A metric that is not written down is a feeling, not a plan. Roster depth Depth is not "more heroes". It is the ability to field a second credible formation without dismantling your first. Build it for a defined purpose: - A defensive formation for raid weeks. - A second damage profile for a different opponent. - A smaller squad for secondary objectives. If you cannot sustain the second squad's healing and replacement costs, you cannot field it repeatedly. Depth without sustain is a one-time burst. Alliance-level impact Advanced play is team infrastructure: - Run the ledger so leadership can see real conversion rates. - Own a phase and train a backup. - Write the after-action note, not just the battle report. - Turn personal experiments into shared doctrine. Monthly reset Once a month, remove one habit: - A spend that consistently underperforms. - A redundant stockpile. - A meeting that produces no decision. - A dashboard nobody reads. Adding is easy. Subtracting is what creates capacity for the next level.

docs.title: Beginner Guide
docs.description: Your first seven days: build a stable economy, pick one hero direction, join an active alliance and stop wasting speed-ups on upgrades you will replace.
docs.content: Your first seven days: build a stable economy, pick one hero direction, join an active alliance and stop wasting speed-ups on upgrades you will replace. The opening week decides whether your account grows smoothly or stalls at every resource wall. Focus on queue uptime, one solid squad and an alliance that communicates. Do not try to win an event in week one. beginner first week progression economy Keep every construction, research and training queue active. Join an active alliance on day one; alliance help and coordination compound immediately. Pick one primary squad direction and stop splitting hero investment. Raise resource production and storage before chasing power. Learn where events live in the UI before spending anything. Complete the tutorial and claim every starter reward before upgrading anything. Join an alliance and read its pinned event plan. Follow the main quest chain until it asks for a resource you cannot produce. Upgrade production buildings and storage in alternating steps. Set a daily routine: claim dailies, fill queues, help alliance, check events. Save speed-ups until you understand which events reward them. Queue length is more valuable than a slightly faster single upgrade. Keep the queue full overnight. Claim alliance help regularly; it is free time. Read the live event screen before spending any saved item. Screenshot your base and resource levels at the end of week one; it becomes your baseline. Ask one experienced member to review your hero lineup. A five-minute review saves a week of wasted shards. Spreading hero shards across every unlocked hero. Rushing the headquarters equivalent without production and storage support. Spending speed-ups outside an event window. Joining a dead alliance for a minor bonus. Ignoring troops and research because construction is more visible. Buying every shop offer that looks discounted. Stabilise the economy Alternate production and storage upgrades. A full queue with capped storage is still wasted capacity; fix the bottleneck first. Commit to one squad Choose a primary damage hero and a front-line hero. Build around them. Ignore the rest until your first squad is functional. Learn the event clock Bookmark the Survival Battle and Alliance Duel screens. Write down one daily reset time and one weekly phase order. Do not spend until you can read both. Join the routine Five minutes twice a day beats an hour once a week: claim dailies, fill queues, help alliance, check events, log off. Construction speed-ups Small reserve High Training speed-ups Small reserve High Research speed-ups Small reserve Core Premium currency Hold Optional Last Asylum: Plague rewards consistency more than bursts. Your first goal is not a high power score; it is a self-sustaining account that can participate in events without draining its future. The first-week checklist Day Focus Do not do --- --- --- 1 Tutorial, alliance, starter rewards Spend premium currency 2 Production and storage balance Rush combat upgrades 3 First squad direction Spread hero shards 4 Research basics and troop tiers Empty speed-up reserve 5 Join an alliance event window Assume a fan schedule is live 6 Review bottlenecks and queues Chase every red dot 7 Screenshot baseline and set routine Compare yourself to veterans What "progress" actually means Power is a symptom, not a strategy. The three engines that carry an account are: 1. Queue uptime — builders, researchers and trainers always working. 2. Resource conversion — turning production into the next useful upgrade. 3. Event timing — spending saved items when they score. A player who logs in twice a day with full queues will outperform a player who logs in constantly but leaves everything idle. Hero direction without overthinking You do not need a perfect roster in week one. You need a functioning squad: - One hero who can absorb damage. - One hero who can deal meaningful damage. - One support or utility slot if available. - A plan to finish the next breakpoint before starting a new hero. Community sources describe battles with up to five heroes. Treat the squad as a system: a second damage hero with no front line is not an upgrade. Speed-ups: save first, spend later New players receive a pile of speed-ups and immediately use them to rush the visible upgrade. Resist. Speed-ups are event currency. Their value is highest when a scored phase rewards the action they accelerate. Rule of thumb for week one: - Use only the speed-ups needed to prevent an overnight queue gap. - Keep a small reserve for a live event you actually understand. - Never spend premium currency to finish a timer that will complete while you sleep. Join the conversation An alliance wiki only works if members contribute. If you find a better route, a mistake, or a screenshot that clarifies a step, send it to leadership. The admin guide explains how content is updated.

docs.title: Construction Priorities
docs.description: Queue order is a strategy. Build toward the next real unlock, stage completions for scored windows and stop upgrading buildings that do not change your account.
docs.content: Queue order is a strategy. Build toward the next real unlock, stage completions for scored windows and stop upgrading buildings that do not change your account. Construction is the most visible form of progress and the easiest place to waste speed-ups. Plan a two-step queue: the prerequisite you need next, then the upgrade that unlock supports. construction buildings queue priority ava Protect the builder queue uptime above all else. Build toward prerequisites for your next meaningful unlock. Stage long timers so they can complete inside a scoring window. Do not upgrade a building with no current use. Coordinate discretionary completions around Alliance Duel Construction phase. List the next three unlocks you actually need. Map their building prerequisites and levels. Keep one short upgrade available as a queue filler. Hold instant-finish items for scored completions. Freeze non-essential completions before AvA start. Record time and resource cost per upgrade. Prerequisite chains matter more than individual building levels. Keep one short upgrade ready to fill a queue gap. A completed building that is not scored is still useful; a speed-up spent outside a window is not. Do not neglect storage and production for a combat building you cannot support. Screenshot the queue before an AvA phase so you know exactly what completes when. Upgrading a building just because it is available. Letting a long timer finish hours before the scoring phase opens. Spending all instant finishes on a non-scored building. Ignoring storage caps while chasing a combat unlock. Starting a long build on Friday without checking the weekend event plan. No record of which upgrades are cheap queue fillers. Map the next unlock Write the target, its prerequisites and the cheapest path. Build the path, not the most impressive building. Stage the completion Time long builds so they can complete inside the matching scoring phase. Keep one short build as a filler. Close the loop After the phase, restart the queue immediately and log what scored. Update the next plan with the actual points. Build speed-ups Reserve for Construction phase Core Construction resources Match the next two upgrades High Builder queue slots Keep filled Core Instant finish items Hold for scoring High A construction priority list copied from a max-level player can stall your economy. Priorities are relative to your current bottlenecks, roster and event plan. The two-step queue At any moment, your construction queue should contain: 1. The next real unlock — a prerequisite or upgrade that changes what you can do. 2. A filler — a cheap, short upgrade to keep the queue busy if the main build completes while you are offline. This prevents both idle builders and accidental long completions. Priority ladder Priority Building type Why --- --- --- 1 Economy production Funds everything else 2 Storage Prevents overflow waste 3 Unlock prerequisites Opens new systems and capacity 4 Training / research capacity Improves event throughput 5 Combat / defence Matters, but only with support 6 Cosmetic / low-use Last AvA construction phase Construction completions are a community-reported scoring source in the Alliance Duel Construction phase. That creates three rules: - Do not complete discretionary upgrades on the day before the phase. - Stage long timers to finish inside the window. - Keep a small instant-finish reserve for the final hour. When to break the plan Priorities change when: - A new unlock requires a different prerequisite. - A balance update changes a building's value. - Your alliance changes its event target. - A storage or production bottleneck is actively blocking progress. Breaking the plan for a red dot is not a priority change. Breaking it for a measured bottleneck is.

docs.title: Hero Development
docs.description: Build a squad, not a collection. Plan breakpoints, protect universal shards and stop paying for power that does not change a battle.
docs.content: Build a squad, not a collection. Plan breakpoints, protect universal shards and stop paying for power that does not change a battle. Hero investment is the least reversible spend on your account. Decide the role you need, finish the breakpoint, and only then start the next project. Event banners are not a roster plan. heroes shards skills breakpoints roster Define a five-slot squad with clear roles before spending shards. Finish star/skill breakpoints instead of levelling everything evenly. Protect universal shards for a hero that changes your squad. Hold recruitment items for hero-scoring event windows. Review the roster after balance changes, not after every banner. List your current heroes, stars, skills and role coverage. Identify the weakest role in your main squad. Choose one hero and one next breakpoint. Calculate the shard and material cost before spending. Set a stop threshold for the current event. Log the result and the score gained. A star breakpoint that unlocks a skill is usually worth more than raw stat levels. Do not upgrade a hero you would not field in your main or second squad. Keep one unassigned universal-shard reserve for a future must-have hero. Use low-stakes battles to test a new hero before committing event resources. Screenshot before/after battle reports to verify the upgrade actually helped. Chasing every new banner and finishing nothing. Upgrading a second damage hero when the front line dies instantly. Spending universal shards on a temporary event bonus. Opening recruitment items before a scoring window. Ignoring skills because star levels look more exciting. Treating power score as proof of battle performance. Audit the roster Build a simple table: hero, role, stars, key skill, next breakpoint, priority. You cannot plan around gaps you have not written down. Pick the weak link Choose the role that causes losses: a dying front line, insufficient damage or missing utility. One upgrade that fixes a loss is worth three cosmetic power gains. Spend inside the window If the Hero phase or a hero event is live or imminent, hold. Spend once, log the points and the shard cost, then stop at the threshold. Hero shards Breakpoint-dependent Core Universal shards Hold for priority heroes Core Skill materials One hero at a time High Recruitment items Hold for scored windows High Gold / upgrade currency Match the breakpoint budget High Do not ask "how high can I take this hero?" Ask "what is the next breakpoint, and what does it unlock?" A hero stuck one star below a skill unlock is often less useful than a lower-power hero with a complete kit. Roster roles A functional squad generally needs coverage for: - Front line / sustain — survives the opening rounds. - Primary damage — converts the front line's time into kills. - Secondary damage or utility — fills the gap the main carry cannot. - Support / control — keeps the squad alive or disrupts the enemy. Exact roles depend on the hero pool and current balance. The principle does not: coverage beats collection . Investment ladder Stage Goal Stop when --- --- --- Unlock Get the hero Do not spend universal shards on a bench hero Functional Complete the core kit Next upgrade is only raw stats Breakpoint Unlock star/skill tier Cost exceeds event reward value Specialist Optimise for a mode You have no defined use case Universal shards Universal shards are the most flexible resource in the game and the easiest to waste. Keep them for: - A hero that completes a role gap. - A breakpoint that unlocks a skill you need. - A limited-time hero that will remain relevant. Do not use them to finish a hero you will replace next week. Testing an upgrade Before and after screenshots are not bureaucracy. They are how you learn: 1. Capture the battle report before the upgrade. 2. Upgrade one variable only. 3. Run a comparable battle. 4. Compare damage, survival and outcome. 5. Keep the result or revert the plan. Event overlap Hero investment is a scoring source in Alliance Duel's Hero phase and in hero-focused events. The best time to spend is when both score the same action — but only if the upgrade is already in your roster plan. An event is a multiplier, not a reason.

docs.title: Research Priorities
docs.description: Research compounds quietly. Sequence economy and combat branches around your next unlock, keep the lab busy, and stage completions for Tech phase.
docs.content: Research compounds quietly. Sequence economy and combat branches around your next unlock, keep the lab busy, and stage completions for Tech phase. Research is a long-horizon investment with short-horizon event value. Pick a branch, finish the useful nodes, keep the lab running, and hold completions for the Tech scoring window when appropriate. research technology queue economy combat Keep the research queue active at all times. Finish economy and capacity nodes that unblock production. Sequence combat research around your actual troop and hero plan. Hold research speed-ups and chests for scored windows. Stop researching nodes you cannot use yet. Map the current research tree and mark three target nodes. Identify prerequisites and total time for each target. Start the longest useful node before logging off. Keep one short node available as a queue filler. Coordinate completions with Tech phase. Log the points and resources per research completion. Read the node effect, not the power score it awards. A short filler node prevents overnight queue gaps. Do not start a long node right before a scoring window unless it can complete inside it. Economy research is event infrastructure: it funds every later spend. Review the tree after every unlock; new branches change the optimal path. Researching a combat node with no matching troop plan. Letting the lab sit idle overnight. Spending research speed-ups outside the scored window. Chasing the most expensive node instead of the next prerequisite. Ignoring capacity and production nodes because they do not look exciting. No record of which nodes are cheap fillers. Choose the branch Decide whether the next unlock is economic (production, capacity, gathering) or combat (troops, heroes, defence). Do not alternate randomly. Stage the completion Time the final node to complete inside a scoring window. Keep a short node ready if the main research finishes early. Verify the effect After completing the node, check the actual stat change and whether it improves a battle or production rate. Keep or adjust the plan. Research speed-ups Reserve for Tech phase Core Research resources Two nodes ahead High Research queue uptime Continuous Core Research chests Hold for scored windows High Research trees, prerequisites and node effects change with updates. Use this guide for sequencing logic, then verify the current tree in-game. The research queue test At any login, ask: - Is the lab researching something useful? - Will it finish before or after my next login? - Does that completion time matter for an event? - Is there a cheap filler node if not? If the answer to the first question is no, fix that before anything else. Branch sequencing Economy first when... - Production is capping or storage is overflowing. - You cannot sustain the next construction tier. - Gathering throughput is your bottleneck. - A capacity node unlocks a useful new action. Combat first when... - Your main squad has a defined troop tier and hero carry. - A specific node unlocks a meaningful battle stat. - Raid phase or a state event is the next major objective. - You can afford the healing and replacement cost. Combat research is a multiplier. If your economy cannot replace losses, a combat node is a temporary high. Build the infrastructure that lets you use the multiplier repeatedly. Research and event scoring Community guides report research completions and research Might as Alliance Duel Tech-phase scoring sources. The practical rules: 1. Do not complete a discretionary research node before Tech phase. 2. Stage the final node so it can finish inside the window. 3. Keep research speed-ups for the phase rather than using them as queue filler. 4. Screenshot the point gain to build your own conversion table. A two-week planning horizon Research takes time. Plan at least two weeks ahead: - Week 1: prerequisites and economy nodes. - Week 2: target node and combat support. - Event weeks: align completions, not starting points, with Tech phase. Finish the plan before starting it. Half-finished research is just a slower version of no research.

docs.title: Resource Management
docs.description: A reserve-first economy for event players: production uptime, storage headroom, and a written floor you do not cross before Alliance Duel.
docs.content: A reserve-first economy for event players: production uptime, storage headroom, and a written floor you do not cross before Alliance Duel. Most resource problems are planning problems. Keep production running, avoid overflow, and separate your event budget from your AvA reserve. The goal is not a bigger bank; it is a bank that never blocks the next scored action. resources economy stockpile reserve production Keep production buildings running and below storage caps. Alternate economy and storage upgrades so neither bottlenecks the other. Maintain a written AvA reserve floor. Spend first on queue uptime, then on scoring actions. Do not liquidate long-term reserves for short-term event tiers. Audit current storage, production and consumption per day. Identify the bottleneck: capacity, production or conversion. Set an AvA reserve floor for each resource. Create an event budget from the excess only. Move speed-up rewards back into queue uptime. Review the budget after every major event. Empty storage is wasted production; full storage is wasted time. Stay between the two. Write the reserve floor down. A number you remember changes under pressure. Upgrade the bottleneck, not the resource with the biggest number. Do not spend speed-ups to produce resources you do not need for the next event. Keep one small emergency reserve in unclaimed rewards if your game mode allows it. Letting production cap overnight. Upgrading storage when production is the actual bottleneck. Spending the AvA reserve on a resource event. Gathering the wrong resource because the node was convenient. Ignoring consumption: a big stockpile that vanishes in one upgrade is not stable. Treating reward speed-ups as free; they are next week's scoring potential. Find the bottleneck Compare daily production, storage cap and planned spending. Fix whichever one stops the others from running. Set the reserve floor Choose the minimum stockpile required to enter AvA with a credible score. Everything above it is event budget. Cycle efficiently Fill queues, claim inside scoring windows, reinvest reward speed-ups, and rebuild the reserve before the next cycle. Production buildings Always running Core Storage capacity Above overnight production High Gather survivors Active rotation High Speed-ups Reserve for scored windows Core Event budget = stockpile − reserve floor. If that number is small, your event spend is small. This one rule prevents most post-event resource crashes. The three-bucket model Every resource sits in one of three buckets: Bucket Purpose Spending rule --- --- --- Reserve AvA, defence, emergency Never spent on optional events Pipeline Queues and production Replenished continuously Budget Current event excess Spend inside the scored window If you cannot tell which bucket a resource is in, it is not budget. Production uptime Resources only appear when production runs. Check: - Are all production buildings staffed and active? - Is storage capacity at least one login interval above production? - Are gather teams on the right node type? - Is anything capped right now? Fixing uptime usually beats a temporary gather boost. It is free, repeatable and compounds. Storage and the overflow trap A large stockpile feels safe until it caps. Overnight overflow is invisible waste. Two habits fix it: 1. Upgrade storage before a long offline period. 2. Spend the overflow on a useful queue, not on a random upgrade. A big bank that blocks storage is not an achievement. It is an unspent production bonus. Convert it into queue uptime or a planned scored action. Event spending order When a scored window opens, spend in this order: 1. Free actions — natural regeneration, existing queues, alliance help. 2. Cheap threshold actions — smallest spend that clears the next tier. 3. Planned reserve release — only on the coordinator's call. 4. Never the AvA floor. Weekly review Every week, answer three questions: - Did production ever cap? Why? - Did any event spend breach the reserve floor? - Which reward converted into the most queue uptime? Write the answers next to your plan. Resource management improves through feedback, not willpower.

docs.title: Troop Development
docs.description: Train with a purpose: tier coverage, batch timing and battle reports that tell you which troops are actually earning their keep.
docs.content: Train with a purpose: tier coverage, batch timing and battle reports that tell you which troops are actually earning their keep. Troop development is a throughput problem wrapped in a combat problem. Keep training queues busy, build the tiers your squad can support, and validate lineups with battle reports instead of assumptions. troops training combat tiers queue Keep the training queue active whenever resources allow. Maintain enough lower-tier troops for events and gathering without sacrificing your main army. Upgrade troop tiers only when you can support them with heroes, research and resources. Test troop matchups with controlled reports. Hold training speed-ups for Preparation / Survival Battle windows. Check training capacity and queue slots. Set a batch size that completes before your next login. Keep a reserve of training speed-ups for scored windows. Review the last ten battle reports for loss patterns. Adjust tier composition based on evidence, not guesswork. Coordinate training with the AvA Preparation phase. Shorter batches reduce overflow waste when capacity is limited. Do not train a tier you cannot equip or support with research. Keep enough troops at home for defence while your main army is out. Use battle reports from both wins and losses. Wins hide inefficiencies. Training during a scoring window is free value if the troops were already in your plan. Training the highest visible tier regardless of support systems. Letting the queue idle overnight. Sending the entire army out and leaving the base undefended. Ignoring healing costs before Raid phase. Judging a troop change from a single battle. Spending every speed-up outside a scoring window. Set the queue rhythm Choose a batch size that completes before your next login. A finished batch that sits idle is wasted capacity. Test the lineup Fight a comparable opponent with a controlled composition. Compare two battle reports before changing your entire army. Coordinate the spend Move training speed-ups into Preparation / Survival Battle scoring windows only when the troops are part of the plan. Food / troop resources Continuous Core Training speed-ups Reserve for scoring windows High Training capacity Upgrade as needed High Healing resources Raid reserve Core Troop tiers and matchups can change with updates. Use the matrix as a living document: record the patch/date next to every conclusion. The throughput rule Troops are produced by time. If the queue is idle, you are losing troops you could have had for free. The first optimisation is not a better tier; it is never leaving the queue empty . A sustainable rhythm looks like: 1. Log in. 2. Claim completed batch. 3. Start the next batch sized to finish before the next login. 4. Use alliance help. 5. Log off. Only after that baseline is stable should you optimise composition. Tier discipline Higher tiers are not automatically better value. Consider: - Support systems: research, hero buffs and equipment that affect the tier. - Resource cost: can your economy sustain a full batch? - Healing cost: can you replace losses after a fight? - Event requirements: some scoring actions care about training volume, not tier. - Defence: a smaller high-tier army on the map leaves the base exposed. A mixed army that keeps your base defended, your events scored and your rallies filled is usually stronger than a perfect single-tier army you cannot sustain. Reading a battle report Look for patterns, not one number: Signal What it suggests --- --- Front line dies early Hero/troop tank gap, or bad matchup High damage but low kills Overkill, target selection or squishy carry Losses spike after round 1 Sustain or healing problem Win with heavy losses Not sustainable for Raid phase Loss with favorable delta Composition may still be improving Capture the report and tag it with the patch, opponent type and composition. A battle report without context is just a screenshot. Preparation for AvA Training speed-ups are a scored resource in the Preparation phase (community-reported). Keep a reserve, but do not train troops you would not otherwise want. Score should follow a useful army, not create one you cannot heal.

docs.title: Advanced Strategy Guide
docs.description: For leaders and analysts: build a decision system, read opponents, allocate stockpiles across phases and turn after-action reviews into doctrine.
docs.content: For leaders and analysts: build a decision system, read opponents, allocate stockpiles across phases and turn after-action reviews into doctrine. Replace reactive event play with a documented decision system that assigns limited stockpiles to the phases where the alliance has the highest expected score advantage. advanced doctrine opponent analysis leadership planning Define an objective for the week and a score target per phase. Allocate stockpiles by expected points per resource, not by emotion. Study the opponent's historical phase strengths. Assign a closer and a reserve before the event starts. Run a 15-minute after-action review within 24 hours. Update the alliance doctrine after every cycle. Two or more weeks of score and spend data. A named analyst or archivist. Authority for a closer to release the reserve. A communication channel with reliable reach. Allocate to your comparative advantage, not to the phase everyone talks about. Use early pressure to force a response, then hold a counter-push reserve. Cap spend per member so the reserve survives unexpected phases. Rotate roles to prevent fatigue and single points of failure. Standardise the review format so data is comparable week to week. The opponent's habits are a resource. Record their phase starts and spend rhythm. A plan with explicit stop conditions outperforms a plan with more effort. Do not change doctrine mid-event unless the scoreboard demands it. Publish the reasoning. Members follow decisions they understand. The best alliances lose less, not just win more. Copying a top alliance's plan without their account depth. Spreading spend evenly across all phases instead of concentrating. No stop condition, so the reserve disappears in the first hour. Leaders making every call personally until burnout. Reviewing only wins and ignoring close losses. Changing the plan every week, so nothing can be measured. Expected vs actual points Per phase Forecast accuracy is a leadership skill. Reserve utilisation ≤ 20% early Hold the closer budget. Participation by phase Tracked Find the phase where attendance collapses. Process changes / month 1–2 Too many changes cannot be evaluated. An advanced alliance is not one that always has the biggest stockpile. It is one that knows where to spend, who decides, and when to stop. Write it down, run it, review it. The decision system For each event week, define: 1. Objective: rank target, milestone floor, or development week. 2. Phase allocation: percentage of stockpile per phase. 3. Stop conditions: score threshold, reserve floor, time limit. 4. Authority: who can change the allocation mid-event. 5. Review time: when the data will be examined. If any of the five is missing, the plan will drift. Opponent analysis Track the opposing alliance across weeks: Signal What it tells you --- --- Fast phase start They front-load; hold a counter-push Late spike They save for the final hour; pressure earlier Weak phase Allocate stockpile to exploit it Overcommitment Let them spend, then win a later phase Member concentration Target coordination, not raw score One result is an anecdote. Three or more weeks is a pattern. Keep the dated evidence. Allocating scarce stockpiles Use expected value: Expected points = action points × probability the phase is contested × strategic multiplier The strategic multiplier accounts for: - Daily phase win value. - Total score pressure. - Member morale. - Future stockpile needs. You will never have perfect numbers. A rough, written ranking beats an intuitive equal split. The final hour The last 60 minutes is a separate sub-game: - The closer has authority to release the reserve. - Everyone else stops spending unless called. - Score updates every 10 minutes. - Screenshots are taken before reset. - The after-action note is written the next day, not in the heat of the moment. Doctrine library Keep a small set of repeatable plays: - Early pressure — score fast, force a response, hold reserve. - Silent bank — low early spend, large final-hour push. - Phase sacrifice — concede a phase, win two others efficiently. - Coverage play — flood a neglected phase with mid-power members. - Defensive week — protect rank, rebuild stockpile, skip optional spends. Each play has prerequisites and risks. Write them down so a new captain can run them without reinventing the plan.

docs.title: Alliance Growth
docs.description: Build an alliance that survives roster churn: clear roles, one communication channel, fair contribution rules and leaders who document decisions.
docs.content: Build an alliance that survives roster churn: clear roles, one communication channel, fair contribution rules and leaders who document decisions. Create a stable, high-participation alliance with defined roles, predictable event routines and a fair path for members of different account sizes. alliance growth recruitment roles leadership Write a one-page alliance charter: schedule, expectations, communication. Assign named roles: commander, phase captains, recruiter, archivist. Set a weekly event routine and publish it before reset. Create contribution paths for low, mid and high-power members. Track attendance and effort, not only raw score. Review and rotate roles every month. A communication channel all members can access. A written event schedule with time zones. A simple contribution ledger. At least two people able to lead an event phase. Recruit for time-zone coverage and reliability before raw power. Publish decisions, not just outcomes. Members follow process they understand. Give newer members a visible, low-cost role in every event. Rotate captains to prevent burnout and single points of failure. Celebrate efficient play, not only spending. A reliable mid-power player is often more valuable than an inconsistent high-power one. One pinned plan beats ten chat messages. Use the same event checklist every week; familiarity reduces missed windows. Ask for feedback after a loss. Silent leadership loses members. Document the roster and roles in the wiki, not only in chat. Recruiting only by power and ignoring activity windows. Leadership decisions made in private and announced as orders. Punishing low scores without accounting for available stockpile. No backup captain when the primary is offline. Changing the plan mid-event without explanation. Letting the alliance culture become a second job. Active event participation Target 70%+ Track by phase, not just weekly login. Phase captain coverage 2 per phase Primary and backup. Median contribution Rising Median matters more than the top spender. Roster churn Falling Review reasons for departures. Recruitment fills slots. Retention builds an alliance. The work is mostly boring: clear expectations, reliable routines, fair recognition, documented decisions. The one-page charter Every alliance needs a document a new member can read in five minutes: - Schedule: reset time, event windows, voice windows. - Expectations: minimum participation, communication, spend discipline. - Roles: who calls what, who to ask. - Culture: how mistakes are handled, how contributions are recognised. - Links: wiki, Discord, calendar. If the charter takes more than a page, it will not be read. Roles that prevent failure Role Responsibility Backup required --- --- --- Commander Final decisions, diplomacy Yes Phase captain Target, spend call, final push Yes Recruiter Pipeline, onboarding No Archivist Screenshots, after-action notes Yes Analyst Scoring ledger, conversion rates No Every critical role needs a second person. Single-point leadership is the most common cause of a collapsed event week. Contribution paths Raw score is the easiest metric to track and the worst one to use alone. Offer roles for different accounts: - High power: rally lead, frontline combat, contested objective. - Mid power: reinforcement, secondary objective, phase co-captain. - Low power: scouting, logistics, documentation, defence rotation. - Non-combat: scheduling, recruitment, wiki upkeep. A member who scouts for every Raid phase is contributing. Say so publicly. Communication routine A predictable rhythm reduces anxiety and duplicate work: - Sunday: publish the week plan. - Daily reset: confirm the phase and target. - Mid-phase: one status update with the score delta. - Final hour: closer call. - Next day: short after-action note. One channel, one pinned plan, one owner. More channels create more noise, not more coordination. Handling a losing week Losing is data. Run a 15-minute review: 1. What was the target? 2. What did we actually score per phase? 3. Where did participation drop? 4. Was the plan clear? 5. What is one change for next week? Do not turn the review into a blame session. The goal is one process improvement, not a scapegoat.

docs.title: Battle Planning
docs.description: Plan the fight before the rally: target priority, squad roles, travel time and a report review that changes the next decision.
docs.content: Plan the fight before the rally: target priority, squad roles, travel time and a report review that changes the next decision. Win more engagements per stamina by choosing targets with a clear purpose, coordinating rally timing and reviewing reports for the next plan. battle rally targets combat reports Define the objective before selecting a target. Scout or inspect the target's defence and support. Assign rally lead, fillers and travel-time cutoffs. Keep a second wave and healing reserve. Capture every battle report with context. Review one variable at a time. A functioning main squad and a secondary formation if available. Stamina and healing reserve. Rally lead with a reliable online window. A target list agreed with leadership. Attack targets that advance the event objective, not just easy wins. Cap filler travel time so the rally does not wait on one member. Use the minimum force that secures the objective; overkill wastes stamina. Keep heal speed-ups for the second wave. Record the opponent's support patterns before committing. The best target is one that scores and is likely to be defended poorly. Rally timing is a team skill; practice it on a low-stakes target. A battle report without composition context is not evidence. Do not chase revenge. Chase the objective. Rotate rally leads to build depth. Launching before all fillers are in travel range. Attacking a target with no event value. Sending the entire army and leaving the base exposed. No healing reserve for the second wave. Judging a composition from one report. Ignoring enemy reinforcements because the initial scout looked weak. Stamina per objective point Tracked The core combat efficiency metric. Rally fill rate Target 90%+ Measure the final join window. Second-wave readiness Heal reserve held Losing the second wave often loses the phase. Reports archived Every major fight Context matters more than volume. "Who can we hit?" is the wrong first question. "What does this hit score, and what will it cost?" is the right one. Target selection is resource allocation with guns. Pre-fight brief Every rally should have a five-line brief: 1. Objective: what this attack achieves. 2. Target: coordinates and expected defence. 3. Launch time: when the rally leaves. 4. Join cutoff: latest travel time for fillers. 5. Second wave: who leads it and with what reserve. If the brief takes longer than the fight, the fight is not planned. Most rally failures are timing failures. Members join late, the rally launches underfilled, or the lead waits so long that the target reinforces. Publish the join cutoff in the same time zone as your members. Target priority Target type Value Risk --- --- --- Event objective High Defended heavily Undefended resource node Low–medium Low, but may not score Enemy rally lead High Counter-rally Support / reinforcement source Medium–high Requires coordination Revenge target Low Emotion-driven, often inefficient Rally discipline - One lead per rally. - One target per rally. - One channel for calls. - A hard join cutoff. - A second wave planned before the first lands. - A screenshot of the report. Duplicate rallies are the fastest way to waste an alliance's stamina. Battle report review Read reports in pairs when possible: - Before and after an upgrade. - Your composition vs. a comparable opponent. - First wave vs. second wave. Look for: - Front-line survival time. - Damage concentration. - Overkill and wasted attacks. - Healing cost relative to objective value. - Whether the win was repeatable. When to disengage Stop the engagement when: - The objective is already secured. - The healing cost exceeds the reward. - The enemy has reinforced beyond your second wave. - Your rally lead is offline. - The event window is closing. A disciplined retreat preserves the army for the next phase. A revenge rally preserves nothing.

docs.title: Event Optimisation
docs.description: A repeatable system for stacking scoreboards: verify, map, stage, spend, log. Built for players who want value per resource, not busywork.
docs.content: A repeatable system for stacking scoreboards: verify, map, stage, spend, log. Built for players who want value per resource, not busywork. Convert a fragmented event calendar into a small number of high-value spend windows, using verified overlap and a written reserve policy. events optimisation overlap scoring efficiency Verify all live event rules at the start of the week. Build a single overlap map instead of separate event plans. Assign one primary scoreboard per day. Stage long actions so completions land in the overlap. Keep a final-hour reserve. Log the results and remove one low-value habit. Access to the live event tabs for every active system. A stockpile snapshot by category. A written reserve floor from leadership. A shared channel for phase calls. Use natural regeneration and free actions first. Prefer actions that score on two boards. Stop at the threshold where the next reward is worth less than the spend. Batch similar actions inside one window instead of trickling them. Protect the highest-value stockpile for the most contested phase. Review the reward preview, not the event banner. Events are not a checklist. They are a portfolio of spend opportunities. A 'good' event can be a bad spend if the next event needs the same stockpile. Write the plan in the second person: 'Spend X on Y at Z time.' Vague plans fail. Take screenshots of the rule screen, not just the scoreboard. If you cannot verify the overlap, assume it does not exist. Planning from memory instead of live screens. Treating every event as equally important. Spending at the start of a window because it feels urgent. Ignoring personal milestones for marginal alliance score. No post-event review, so the same mistake repeats. Using premium currency to bridge a threshold that does not return the value. Overlap windows used 3–5 / week More is not always better; quality beats quantity. Reserve breach 0 The only acceptable number for the AvA floor. Reward value / spend Improving Compare against last week's ledger. Unplanned completions Verify → Map → Stage → Spend → Log. Skip a step and the plan becomes a guess. Repeat the loop weekly and the alliance builds a real conversion dataset. 1. Verify Open every live event tab. Capture: - Phase/theme order. - End time in UTC and local time. - Scored actions. - Reward preview. - Eligibility. Community schedules are leads, not evidence. If the live screen contradicts a guide, the live screen wins. 2. Map Put every active event on one weekly grid. Mark: - Hard windows — fixed start/end times. - Soft windows — phases that last a day. - Intersections — actions that score twice. - Dead zones — times with no valuable scoring. Separate plans create conflicts. A single map shows which stockpile is wanted by two events at the same time — the most important thing to know. 3. Stage Most high-value actions take hours. Stage them: - Start long timers early enough to finish inside the window. - Keep a cheap filler action for queue gaps. - Hold instant-finish items and speed-ups for the final adjustment. - Screenshot the timer so the next stage is factual. 4. Spend Use the hierarchy: 1. Free actions. 2. Cheapest threshold-clearing action. 3. Planned overlap spend. 4. Closer reserve. 5. Never the reserve floor. 5. Log A minimal ledger is enough: Date Event Action Cost Points Reward Note --- --- --- --- --- --- --- 2026-10-20 AvA + SB 12h build finish 2× 1h ? Tier 3 Landed in overlap After four weeks, you will know which actions are worth repeating and which are theatre. The portfolio mindset Rank events by value per resource , not by excitement: - Alliance rank events usually justify the biggest spend. - Personal ladders are good for guaranteed milestones. - Limited-time shops are worth it only if the primary reward is reachable. - Cosmetic or low-tier rewards should not touch the reserve. If an event does not fit the portfolio this week, skip it deliberately. Skipping is a strategy, not a failure.

docs.title: Free-to-Play Guide
docs.description: Compete without a credit card: protect premium currency, farm queue uptime, choose events with guaranteed value and let bigger accounts overspend on rank.
docs.content: Compete without a credit card: protect premium currency, farm queue uptime, choose events with guaranteed value and let bigger accounts overspend on rank. Build a competitive account by converting free actions and guaranteed event milestones into steady progression, while refusing low-value rank races. free to play f2p premium currency value efficiency Set a premium currency floor and spend only above it. Prioritise guaranteed milestone rewards over uncertain rankings. Use the event overlap map to double-dip free actions. Keep queues full; queue uptime is the F2P engine. Spend speed-ups only to hit a reward threshold, not for convenience. Track value per premium unit and remove leaks monthly. Discipline with premium currency and speed-ups. A daily routine that fits your schedule. Access to the live event screens and alliance plan. A ledger of what you spend and earn. Farm guaranteed milestones; ignore leaderboard prestige unless the reward is exceptional. Use natural regeneration before any speed-up. Convert event rewards into queue uptime, not vanity power. Choose one main squad and one secondary role; do not chase banners. Let whales fight for rank while you take the guaranteed tiers. The best F2P purchase is usually more queue uptime, not a one-time power spike. If a reward tier is unreachable without premium currency, it is not your tier. Keep a premium floor for an emergency upgrade or a genuinely broken value offer. Screenshot your currency before and after an event; leaks become obvious. A skipped event is cheaper than a bad spend. Spending premium currency to bridge a small score gap for a low-value reward. Chasing every new hero banner. Using speed-ups because waiting is annoying. Ignoring guaranteed daily milestones while chasing rank. Buying random discounted shop items with no plan. Comparing your account to a whale's account. Premium currency floor Set and hold A fixed reserve for emergency value. Guaranteed milestones claimed Maximise The core F2P income stream. Queue uptime 90%+ The cheapest progression multiplier. Speed-ups spent outside events Near zero Every one is lost scoring value. Whales compete for ranking rewards. Free-to-play accounts should compete for guaranteed milestones and queue uptime . Those rewards do not depend on someone else spending more than you. The three F2P engines 1. Queue uptime — construction, research and training always running. 2. Guaranteed milestones — daily and event tiers that everyone can reach. 3. Overlap efficiency — one action scoring on two boards. Rank chasing is a fourth, optional engine. It is expensive and inconsistent. Treat it as a bonus, not a plan. Premium currency rules - Set a floor (for example, enough for one emergency upgrade). - Spend only above the floor. - Buy value that compounds: capacity, queue slots, guaranteed progression. - Never bridge a score gap unless the reward exceeds the currency spent. - Wait 24 hours before any unplanned purchase. Limited-time shops are designed to make the last 20% of a reward feel close. If reaching it requires breaking your premium floor, the correct move is to stop. The shop will return; your reserve may not. A weekly F2P routine Day Action Time --- --- --- Daily Claim dailies, fill queues, alliance help 5 min Monday Read phase plan, set stockpile floor 10 min Midweek Check overlap windows, spend only planned actions 10 min Weekend Claim milestones, review ledger 15 min Monthly Remove one leak, update roster plan 30 min What to ignore - Leaderboard drama you cannot influence. - Banners with no roster slot. - Discounts on resources you already overflow. - Events whose rewards do not help your next progression step. - Advice that assumes unlimited speed-ups. Measuring success Track three numbers monthly: - Guaranteed milestones claimed. - Premium currency balance trend. - Main squad and queue progress. If all three are rising, you are winning the F2P game, regardless of where you sit on a whale leaderboard.

Map Survival Battle themes to AvA phases for the current week. Assign each day a primary scoreboard and a secondary scoreboard. Reserve 10–20% of each stockpile for the final-hour closer window. Log points per phase and update the conversion table. Stop spending once the marginal reward drops below the reserve value. Visibility of both live event screens and their current phase order. A stockpile snapshot for construction, research, training, hero and Raven actions. Alliance leadership's AvA target and spend floor. One written weekly plan shared with the alliance. Score the action that appears on both boards, not the one that appears on the louder board. Stack long timers so they complete inside the overlap, not before it. Use free and natural actions first; release saved stockpiles only in the overlap window. Protect the closer reserve; early over-spending destroys optionality. If the scoreboards conflict, choose AvA rank over personal bracket rank. Monday is for mapping, not spending. A 4-hour Survival Battle round is a trigger window; a 24-hour AvA phase is a budget window. Screenshot both boards at the start and end of the overlap. Write down which action scored in both systems. That is your highest-value play. Do not trust a themed rotation you have not seen on your own account this week. Spending a phase stockpile during a Survival Battle round that does not reward it. Assuming the AvA phase order from last week still applies. Blowing the closer reserve in the first two hours. Ignoring the daily Survival Battle milestone because the AvA phase looks more important. Using speed-ups to finish a timer that would complete inside the overlap naturally. Treating overlap as permission to spend more. It is permission to spend better. Combined points / 100 speed-ups Track weekly Your core efficiency metric for overlap actions. Overlap windows identified Target 3+ Construction, research and training are the usual candidates. Closer reserve spent ≤ 20% of budget Held back until the final 60 minutes. Actions outside overlap Minimise Every non-overlap spend needs a specific reason. This guide assumes the community-reported structures: six four-hour Survival Battle rounds per day and a Monday–Saturday Alliance Duel phase order. Both are version- and server-sensitive. Open both live event screens before using any overlap map. The core idea Survival Battle is a short-cycle scoreboard. Alliance Duel is a long-cycle scoreboard. - Survival Battle round: four hours. The action must land inside that round. - Alliance Duel phase: one day. The action must land inside that phase. When the two windows intersect and reward the same action, you get an overlap window . That is the only time a single spend has two chances to earn value. The goal is not to play more events. It is to make the events you already play share the same action. One training batch, one research completion, one construction finish — placed in the intersection. Build the weekly map Do this every Monday: 1. Screenshot the Survival Battle theme order for the day. 2. Screenshot the Alliance Duel phase and current score. 3. Draw a 7-day grid. 4. Put AvA phases across the top. 5. Put Survival Battle themes down the side. 6. Mark intersections where the same action scores on both boards. 7. Assign stockpiles to intersections, not to individual events. 8. Write the closer reserve and the stop conditions. Day AvA phase (verify) Survival Battle theme (verify) Overlap action Budget --- --- --- --- --- Mon Raven Build / training rotation Raven action if both score 20% Tue Construction Research / build rotation Staged construction finish 20% Wed Tech Research / hero rotation Research completion 20% Thu Hero Hero / Raven rotation Planned hero breakpoint 15% Fri Preparation Training rotation Training batch 15% Sat Raid Combat rotation Rally + heal reserve 10% The intersections above are illustrative. Fill in the actual live themes and phases for your week. If an intersection does not exist, do not invent one. The four-hour round rule A Survival Battle round is short. You cannot move a 20-hour construction timer into a four-hour window on a whim. You must stage it: - T-24h: start the long timer. - T-4h: check the remaining time. - T-1h: use a controlled speed-up to land inside the overlapping round. - T-0: complete and claim on both boards. This is why overlap strategy is mostly preparation. The spend happens in seconds; the setup takes a day. Overlap decision tree 1. Do both boards reward this action? - No → Do not spend unless the single-board reward is exceptional. - Yes → Continue. 2. Is the action already planned for the account? - No → Stop. Overlap does not justify a bad upgrade. - Yes → Continue. 3. Is the cheaper threshold action available? - Yes → Use it first. - No → Continue. 4. Will the spend breach the AvA reserve floor? - Yes → Stop. - No → Spend, log, claim. A worked example Suppose Tuesday is both Construction phase and a Build Territory round. - You have a 14-hour build queued since Monday. - It would naturally finish at 06:00 Tuesday, before the overlap round. - You use a small speed-up to finish it at 09:30 instead, inside the round and inside the phase. - You claim both scores and log the resource cost. The win is not the speed-up. The win is that you staged the timer so a small speed-up could move the completion into the intersection.
